newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: AUSTRALIAN MEDIA REFORM UNLIKELY SOON- KEY MP SAYS.
newsitem.headline: AUSTRALIAN MEDIA REFORM UNLIKELY SOON- KEY MP SAYS.

text.p: Reforms to Australia's media ownership laws were unlikely this week, the head of a committee charged with approving any changes said on Tuesday.
Liberal Party backbencher Gary Hardgrave told Australian Broadcasting Corp radio that any Cabnet approval of reforms still had to be approved by his backbench committee on communications.

An announcement this week "is certainly not in keeping with the undertakings that have been given to us as a committee that there would be no decisions made during the break period of the parliament", said Hardgrave.
Cabinet is considering changes to cross ownership limits and government officials have said a decision may be announced as early as Tuesday.
Parliament is due to resume on August 25.
Hardgrave said the committee had been assured there would be no changes announced from the Cabinet meeting.
"That's what we've been told, and I can only take the Minister's word for it," he said.
Under current laws, television station owners are banned from holding more than 15 percent of a newspaper in the same major market, and vice versa.
The Liberal-National government ordered a review of these limits soon after winning office in March 1996.
Hardgrave said the committee would welcome a public inquiry.

"I think that anything that takes it that step further and that is to bring onstream and up to date the people of Australia as to the range of issues involved in this is a good thing," he said. "The process should be as open and as transparent as possible."

Media analysts have been alert to any signals that the government may be about to change media policy as it could affect the ownership of newspaper publisher John Fairfax Holdings Ltd and Seven Network Ltd.

Media barons Kerry Packer, who owns Publishing and Broadcasting Ltd, and Rupert Murdoch, the executive chairman of global media group News Corp Ltd, have lobbied Prime Minister John Howard in recent months about the proposed changes.

Packer's PBL has a 15 percent stake in Fairfax, behind the 22 percent held by Brierley Investments Ltd of New Zealand, and has said it wanted to merge with Fairfax, possibly as soon as Christmas this year.

Murdoch has a 15 percent stake in Seven, the second ranked television group behind Packer's Nine Network, and has talked about raising the stake. Murdoch's newspaper interests in Australia are also enormous, accounting for about 70 percent of circulation in the major capital cities.
